data.title: Frontline Earnings Call Highlights Strong Cash Generation
data.description:
Frontline ((FRO)) has held its Q3 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

Frontline’s earnings call carried a strongly positive tone, supported by exceptional profits, powerful cash generation and ample liquidity. Management also pointed to historically high freight rates and strong fourth-quarter bookings, although it warned that geopolitical risks, weaker Chinese imports and a large tanker order book could create volatility.

Exceptional Q3 Profitability

Frontline reported third-quarter 2026 profit of $641.4 million, or $2.88 per share, while adjusted profit reached $530.9 million, or $2.38 per share. Management said the business was operating at an approximately 90% profit margin, with revenue running at roughly 10 times operating costs.

Strong Spot Market Performance

Third-quarter spot time charter equivalent rates averaged $148,500 per day for VLCCs, $102,500 for Suezmaxes and $67,800 for LR2/Aframax vessels. These figures underline the strength of the tanker market, even though rates declined from their October peaks.

Record Fourth-Quarter Bookings

Frontline had booked 68% of its fourth-quarter VLCC days at $562,600 per day, 69% of Suezmax days at $324,300 and 68% of LR2/Aframax days at $190,800. Management described the quarter as record-breaking, while noting that the figures were based on load-to-discharge days and could change because of quarter-end balance days.

Strong Liquidity Position

Frontline reported $1.4 billion of liquidity, including $1.1 billion of undrawn revolver capacity, marketable securities and required minimum cash. The company has no debt maturities until 2028 and no meaningful maturities until 2031, giving it substantial financial flexibility.

Financing Costs Reduced

Between June and November 2026, Frontline reduced its weighted average interest margin by 60 basis points, from 178 basis points at the end of the first quarter to 118 basis points. Amendments, refinancings, newbuilding financing and asset sales all contributed to the improvement.

Revolver Capacity Expanded

Total revolving credit capacity rose from $473 million at the end of the first quarter to $2.27 billion in the third quarter. Of that amount, $1.2 billion was drawn and $1.1 billion remained available, allowing Frontline to manage liquidity without carrying excessive cash.

Modern and Efficient Fleet

After the remaining VLCC deliveries and the sale of two VLCCs, Frontline expects to operate 14 VLCCs, 19 Suezmaxes and 18 Aframax/LR2 tankers. The fleet’s average age is expected to be 6.9 years, with all vessels classified as eco-ships and 69% fitted with scrubbers.

Low Cash Breakevens

Average cash breakevens for the next 12 months are estimated at $24,100 per day for VLCCs, $25,200 for Suezmaxes and $20,600 for LR2 tankers. The fleet average is approximately $23,600 per day, or $21,800 excluding dry-dock costs, providing protection if rates weaken.

Operating Expenses Declined

Third-quarter operating expenses including dry dock were $8,400 per day for VLCCs, $10,600 for Suezmaxes and $13,400 for LR2 tankers. Fleet-average operating expenses excluding dry dock were $8,100 per day, while total ship operating costs fell by $2.1 million from the previous quarter.

Large Cash Generation Potential

Using its current fleet and market rates as of November 19, Frontline estimated potential cash generation of $4.4 billion, or about $19.70 per share. That figure represents a 44% cash-flow yield at the current share price, and could rise to $5.8 billion if spot rates increase by 30%.

Trade and Inventory Support

Management said global crude exports had moved above September 2025 levels, while Asian imports excluding China were well ahead of seasonal patterns. It also cited expectations for global inventory builds of 4 million barrels per day in 2027 against projected consumption of 104.5 million barrels per day.

Atlantic Basin Opportunity

A gradual shift toward higher Atlantic Basin crude exports could benefit tanker demand by increasing voyage distances. Management said replacing a 1 million-barrel Middle East-to-Asia voyage with an Atlantic-to-Asia movement could lengthen the voyage by 30%, while Middle East cargoes move toward Europe.

Trade Inefficiencies Support Demand

Approximately 70 VLCCs were estimated to be involved in shuttling crude through the Strait of Hormuz. That represents nearly 10% of the fleet below 20 years old and almost 20% of the actively traded fleet, with shuttle activity, ship-to-ship transfers and security delays creating extra vessel days.

Fleet Age Offers a Cushion

Although Frontline’s relevant order book averages 27% of the existing fleet, management said the global tanker fleet’s high average age could absorb some new deliveries. Older ships may move to recycling yards, while current orders point to peak fleet growth of 6% to 7% in 2028.

More Time-Charter Coverage Planned

Frontline said much of its current time-charter coverage is short dated and will begin rolling off in the first quarter. Management expects the company to carry a much higher level of time-charter coverage than in previous years, potentially allowing it to lock in attractive rates.

Newbuilding Funding Secured

Frontline’s remaining newbuilding commitments totaled $288.7 million at the end of September, covering nine vessels acquired from Hemen affiliates. The company secured up to $737 million in financing for all nine newbuildings, reducing funding risk around the fleet expansion.

Adjusted Profit Fell Sequentially

Third-quarter adjusted profit declined by $49.3 million from the previous quarter. Management attributed the decrease mainly to lower time charter equivalent earnings, despite the company continuing to report very strong absolute profitability.

Freight Rates Corrected

Management said freight rates had corrected substantially after reaching extreme levels in October. The decline was linked to increased Middle East oil flows and improved supply conditions, but rates were still described as historically high by industry standards.

Geopolitical Risks Increased

Trading risks rose during the quarter in the Black Sea, Red Sea and around the Gulf of Oman. Management also raised concerns about seafarer safety, environmental exposure and attacks affecting vessels involved in shuttle operations.

Hormuz Operations Face Heavy Inefficiency

Vessels operating in the Hormuz shuttle trade may capture only about half of the TCE implied by the TD3C index. Waiting time, security delays, ship-to-ship transfers and terminal issues reduce earnings, while management said incidents in the trade were occurring frequently and were often underreported.

Near-Term Export Volumes May Weaken

Management said November crude export data would likely be lower than the figures available through October. The worsening security situation around the Strait of Hormuz was expected to have a short-term effect, particularly on U.S. export activity.

China Imports Remain Soft

Chinese crude imports were still running approximately 2 million barrels below the average for the fourth quarter of 2025. The shortfall remains a notable weakness in an otherwise supportive global demand and trade backdrop.

Large Order Book Raises Concern

Frontline described the tanker order book as alarming, with orders averaging 27% across the relevant vessel classes. Management warned that adding 60 or 100 VLCCs to the market in a single year could place considerable pressure on freight rates.

Newbuilding Deliveries Could Pressure Rates

Deliveries are concentrated in the second half of 2027, which management acknowledged could be a challenging period for the market. The company also stressed that tanker conditions would not remain at October levels as additional capacity enters service.

Shipyard Capacity Is Constrained

Some high-cost shipyards that recently expanded capacity are struggling to find skilled workers. Shortages of welders and other qualified personnel, higher labor costs and limits on rapid capacity expansion could restrict the pace of future vessel deliveries.

Time Charters Limit Near-Term Upside

Existing time-charter coverage reduces Frontline’s near-term cash generation compared with the spot market because the time-charter curve is sharply backwardated. However, much of that coverage is expected to roll off beginning in the first quarter, creating an opportunity to reset contracts.

Market Forecasts Remain Uncertain

Management repeatedly described the tanker market as fluid and difficult to forecast. Middle East security, available oil volumes, refinery activity, trade routes and inventory rebuilding all remain uncertain, making precise 2027 VLCC TCE estimates impossible at this stage.

Potential Fleet Losses Tighten Supply

Industry sources cited by management estimated that 1% to 2% of the VLCC fleet was either under repair or potentially becoming a total loss. Such disruptions could temporarily remove additional capacity from the market and partly offset newbuilding deliveries.

Depreciation Increased

Depreciation rose by $4.4 million from the prior quarter following the delivery of six newbuildings during the second and third quarters. Vessel sales partly offset the increase, but the larger fleet contributed to higher non-cash costs.

Supplier Rebates Declined

Lower ship operating expenses were partly offset by a reduction in supplier rebates. Even so, overall operating costs fell during the quarter, helped by vessel sales and lower general running expenses.

Forward Guidance Points to Strong Cash Flow

Frontline expects a record fourth quarter, with most vessel classes already booked at exceptionally high rates, and plans to increase time-charter coverage. Management estimates average cash breakevens of $23,600 per day and potential cash generation of $4.4 billion, or $19.70 per share, with the range moving to $3 billion at 30% lower spot rates and $5.8 billion at 30% higher rates.

Frontline’s earnings call showed a company benefiting from strong tanker rates, low breakevens, a modern fleet and a well-protected balance sheet. While newbuilding supply, geopolitical disruptions and weaker Chinese imports create meaningful risks, management’s cash-generation potential and fourth-quarter bookings leave the overall investment message firmly positive.

data.title: Mr Price Earnings Call Shows Growth Amid Rising Pressure
data.description:
Mr Price Group ((MRPZF)) has held its Q2 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

Mr Price’s earnings call struck a broadly positive but cautious tone. Six straight periods of earnings growth, strong cash generation, margin expansion, store openings and encouraging NKD results were balanced by weak consumer conditions, supply disruptions, higher finance costs and a difficult near-term outlook.

Sixth Consecutive Period of Earnings Growth

Mr Price reported its sixth consecutive period of earnings growth. Diluted headline earnings per share rose 2.2% to 508.6 cents, while dividends per share increased 2%.

Revenue and Operating Profit Lifted by NKD

Group revenue jumped 40.5% to ZAR 26.1 billion, while gross profit rose 69.5% to ZAR 12.1 billion. Operating profit increased 30.7% to ZAR 2.7 billion, with the NKD acquisition contributing materially to the growth rates.

African Operations Outpaced the Market

African revenue increased 2.9% to ZAR 19.1 billion, and retail sales grew 3.1%, ahead of the market’s 1.2% rise. Weighted average space grew 3.8%, units increased 1.6% and retail selling price inflation was 1.4%.

Africa Expanded Margins

African gross profit rose 4.6% to ZAR 7.5 billion, lifting the gross margin by 60 basis points to 40.6%. Expenses increased 3.8%, helping operating profit rise 5.9% and the operating margin improve by 30 basis points to 11.8%.

Disciplined Pricing and Markdown Control

Management credited tight input-cost control and disciplined markdowns for the improvement in Africa’s gross margin. Apparel margin rose to 41.1%, Homeware to 42.8% and Telecoms to 21.9%.

Cost Containment Supported Africa

Employment costs fell 1.1% despite 3.8% growth in weighted average space, helped by flexible remuneration and staffing efficiencies. Excluding a once-off lease adjustment, occupancy costs rose 3.8%, while other operating costs excluding foreign exchange losses increased only 1.1%.

Telecoms Delivered Strong Growth

Telecoms retail sales increased 9.1%, while market share rose 70 basis points, according to GfK. Operating profit grew 9%, despite a comparison with 16.8% growth in the previous year.

Homeware Continued to Improve

Homeware retail sales grew 2.2%, with Mr Price Home and Sheet Street gaining momentum in the second quarter. Yuppiechef continued to outperform the market, while operating profit rose 1.4% against a high double-digit base.

Credit Portfolio Quality Improved

The debtors book grew 5.4% to ZAR 3.1 billion, while net bad debt improved to 8.7% from 8.9%. Credit sales increased 3.7% to ZAR 2.2 billion, and the approval rate rose 30 basis points to 22.9%.

Store Expansion Remained a Priority

The group opened 145 stores during the period, including 101 in Africa, taking the African total to 3,248. Studio 88 reached 1,056 stores, Power Fashion reached 365, and Mr Price Money added seven stand-alone cellular outlets.

New Stores Delivered Strong Returns

Management said returns from new stores again exceeded the group’s threshold for return on operating assets. This performance supports continued investment in stores and reinforces the group’s capital allocation approach.

NKD Produced a Positive Operating Profit

NKD generated revenue of just under ZAR 7.0 billion and operating profit of ZAR 526 million. Its 7.5% operating margin was supported by sales growth ahead of Germany’s total apparel and value markets in both quarters.

NKD Margin Benefited from Stock Discipline

NKD reported gross profit of ZAR 4.6 billion and a 67.4% gross margin. Disciplined stock management, lower markdowns and a strong sourcing model helped protect profitability.

European Cash Flow Reduced Debt

The European business generated ZAR 1.3 billion of cash, covering ZAR 200 million of capital expenditure, ZAR 860 million of lease payments and ZAR 256.8 million of debt repayment. NKD ended the period with ZAR 636 million of cash and ZAR 746 million of bank debt.

German Refinancing Lowered Interest Costs

The group reduced German debt by ZAR 256 million and secured facilities at an interest rate 5.5% below the previous rate. The first-half benefit was limited, but the refinancing improves the cost of debt over time.

NKD Integration Benefits Identified

Management identified potential savings from technology licences, integration work, store closures and other initiatives. These opportunities amount to about ZAR 100 million annually and are additional to those in the original business case.

Logistics Integration Made Progress

Studio 88 was fully integrated into the group’s outbound logistics network, while Yuppiechef’s eastern offshore shipments were consolidated into group processes. Power Fashion is also being moved into the Hammersdale distribution centre.

Cash Generation Supported Investment

The group generated ZAR 4.8 billion of cash during the period, while cash sales accounted for more than 91% of group sales after including NKD. Management said this provides room to invest while maintaining a dividend payout ratio of 63% of headline earnings per share.

Capital Spending Remained Growth-Oriented

First-half capital expenditure was ZAR 619 million, including ZAR 419 million in Africa and ZAR 200 million in Europe. Planned investment is focused on stores and expansion across both regions.

RedCap Targets Efficiency and Growth

The RedCap roadmap is designed to lower the structural cost base, reduce complexity and improve delivery. It also targets better omnichannel services, customer personalisation, technology, data, supply chains and global sourcing.

Distribution Technology Held Costs Steady

Mr Price said the cost per unit processed in South Africa remained unchanged despite upgrades at its Gauteng distribution centre. Technology, systems intelligence and automated bots helped contain operating costs.

No New Acquisitions Are Planned

Management said it has no sizable or small acquisition under consideration. The focus is instead on existing businesses, the RedCap programme and extracting integration benefits from NKD.

NKD’s Newer Stores Performed Well

NKD closed 36 stores as part of its restructuring programme but opened 44. Management said stores opened one, two and three years ago are meeting their objectives and expected returns despite difficult trading conditions.

Consumers Faced Heavy Economic Pressure

High energy and transport costs, weaker consumer confidence, higher borrowing costs and rising inflation weighed on discretionary spending. Fuel prices also reduced the disposable income available to value-focused customers.

Global Uncertainty Remained Elevated

Management described global uncertainty as unusually high, with South African GDP reported at minus 0.2%. Inflation rose by roughly 1% to 1.5% in South Africa and Germany, while interest rates increased by 50 basis points in both markets.

Supply Disruptions Threatened Peak Trading

Vessel shortages, typhoons in Asia and disruption at Durban port reduced stock buffers ahead of the peak season. Inputs that normally arrive around week 47 were expected to move closer to week 49, increasing execution risk.

Black Friday Stock Was Tighter

The group said some areas had less stock than planned because of supply-chain challenges. Certain deliveries could be delayed by up to two weeks, although management expected major final inputs before Christmas.

Finance Expenses Rose Sharply

Finance expenses surged 145.3% to just over ZAR 1.0 billion. Interest on debt rose to ZAR 490 million from ZAR 25 million, while lease interest increased 35% after NKD’s store portfolio was included.

Bottom-Line Growth Was Limited

Profit before tax increased only 1.4% to ZAR 1.8 billion, while profit attributable to owners was flat. Acquisition funding costs, lease interest and other finance expenses absorbed much of the operating profit growth.

Africa Comparable Sales Were Flat

African comparable sales were unchanged, despite 1.6% unit growth and 1.4% selling-price inflation. Management warned that sustaining only about 3% top-line growth in an inflationary environment would not be acceptable for an extended period.

Apparel Profit Declined Despite Sales Growth

Apparel retail sales increased 3%, outperforming the market’s 0.4% growth. However, operating profit fell 0.9% against a high double-digit increase in the previous year.

Financial Services Profit Came Under Pressure

Financial services revenue grew 3.2%, but operating profit declined 3.7%. The result reflected a larger movement in the debtors provision compared with the prior year.

Currency Losses Increased Costs

Other operating costs rose 6.6% to ZAR 1.26 billion, mainly because of foreign exchange losses. Weaker currencies in Botswana, Ghana and Zambia increased the rand cost of the group’s operations.

NKD Faced Weather and Currency Headwinds

Extreme winter snow and prolonged summer heat waves disrupted NKD’s European trading. A weaker euro against the rand and dollar also reduced the rand value of NKD’s reported profits.

NKD Closures Added Restructuring Costs

NKD closed 36 stores during the period and increased its annual closure budget to 90 stores. Management said the targeted locations were loss-making, although the restructuring programme carries closure costs.

Refinancing Costs Offset Early Benefits

NKD incurred once-off refinancing costs of about ZAR 32 million to ZAR 33 million in the first half. These costs were expensed through the income statement and initially offset the benefit of cheaper funding.

Online Performance Needs Improvement

Management acknowledged that online sales had declined and were below the desired level. Better systems functionality and a stronger connection between e-commerce and stores are key priorities under RedCap.

Credit Policy Stayed Conservative

The TransUnion South African Consumer Credit Index moved below 50, indicating unhealthy conditions. Rising food, fuel and borrowing costs led management to maintain a cautious approach to credit until consumers recover.

Near-Term Trading Remained Difficult

Management said the second half would not be easy, citing macroeconomic pressure and supply-chain disruption. It also cautioned against expecting a sudden structural improvement in trading conditions.

Group Net Debt Increased

Closing group net debt was ZAR 7.7 billion following the NKD acquisition, the Studio 88 minority buyout, dividend payments, lease liabilities and short-term facilities. Management described the debt-to-EBITDA range of 1.5 to 1.75 as comfortable.

Guidance Keeps Investment Plans Intact

Full-year capital expenditure is expected at ZAR 1 billion in South Africa and ZAR 400 million in Europe, with about 300 new stores planned across both regions. Africa’s weighted average space growth is expected at 3% to 4%, while the Africa segment’s operating margin guidance is 13% to 15%.

NKD is expected to close 90 stores, with annualised benefits of about ZAR 100 million, while cheaper German refinancing should support the second half and become more meaningful later. data.title: Huhtamaki Earnings Call Signals Resilience Amid Uneven Demand
data.description:
Huhtamaki Oyj ((FI:HUH1V)) has held its Q3 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

Huhtamaki’s earnings call carried a broadly positive tone, despite uneven demand and cost pressures. Comparable sales grew 4%, adjusted EBIT margin reached 10.9%, cash flow remained positive for a sixth straight quarter, and leverage continued to fall, while North America and Foodservice weighed on performance.

Comparable Sales Returned to Growth

Huhtamaki reported 4% comparable net sales growth in the quarter and 2% growth year to date. The result marked a second consecutive quarter of comparable growth despite a very soft demand environment.

Margins and Earnings Per Share Improved

Adjusted EBIT reached EUR 110.5 million, producing a 10.9% margin, while the year-to-date margin was 10.4%. Adjusted EPS rose 10% to EUR 0.68, and year-to-date EPS increased 3% to EUR 1.88.

Cash Flow Stayed Positive

The company recorded its sixth consecutive quarter of positive free cash flow. Management said the progress positioned Huhtamaki for a strong finish to the year, although year-to-date free cash flow remained below the previous year.

Flexible Packaging Delivered Strong Momentum

Flexible Packaging achieved healthy volume growth, passed through raw-material price increases, and benefited from a favorable product mix. Sales and EBIT increased year over year across all regions, while year-to-date cash flow was ahead of last year.

Decentralized Model Supported Flexible Packaging

A decentralized operating model introduced early last year helped Flexible Packaging win local and regional customers. Cost reductions also created a more competitive base, supporting both new business and improved profitability.

Fiber Packaging Grew Profitably

Fiber Packaging delivered 3% comparable growth in the quarter and 5% year to date. Volumes increased across all regions, profitability improved, and demand in egg and food markets was stable or improving, although cup-carrier foodservice markets were weaker.

Hammond Startup Showed Progress

The Hammond startup made significant progress late in the quarter, with better machine speeds and an improved product mix. Management attributed the improvement to operational adjustments and reported positive momentum at the facility.

Improvement Playbook Expands

Huhtamaki is applying the Flexible Packaging playbook to North America and Foodservice through commercial excellence, procurement, and cost-out measures. Its long-term adjusted EBIT margin ambition remains 10%-12%, with North America targeted to return above 10%.

Capital Spending Remained Disciplined

Capital expenditure was in line with last year during the quarter and approximately EUR 20 million lower year to date. The company continued to invest in businesses with growth potential while maintaining tighter capital discipline.

Leverage Continued to Decline

Net debt stood at EUR 1.2 billion, with net debt to EBITDA at 1.9x, below the company’s 2x-3x ambition corridor. Gearing was 0.58x, and management said deleveraging remained a continuing priority.

Liquidity and Financing Profile Strengthened

Huhtamaki ended the quarter with EUR 364 million in cash equivalents and EUR 450 million in unused committed credit facilities. Average debt maturity increased to 3.9 years from 3.6 years at the end of the third quarter of 2025, helped by refinancing and an extended revolving credit facility.

Returns Moved Closer to Strategic Goals

Adjusted return on investments improved to 12.3% from 11.9% a year earlier, while adjusted return on equity reached 13.8%. Management said the company was meeting its ambitions for adjusted EBIT margin, net debt to EBITDA, and dividend payout.

North America Retained Customers and Share

Despite weak North American demand, management said Huhtamaki had not lost market share or customers compared with the same quarter last year. The company is therefore treating the weakness primarily as a demand and execution challenge rather than a competitive loss.

M&A and Buybacks Remain Options

Management said it remains active in the mergers and acquisitions market but will apply strict strategic and financial criteria. If suitable acquisitions are not found, the board could consider share buybacks.

North American Seasonality Offers Support

Management expects fourth-quarter seasonality in North American retail to be significantly stronger than in the third quarter. Halloween, Thanksgiving, and Christmas were identified as important seasonal supports for demand.

North American Sales Fell Sharply

North American comparable sales declined 9% in the quarter and 3% year to date. Foodservice demand was very weak, retail was also soft, and management pointed to low consumer confidence as a major factor.

Volume and Freight Costs Hit EBIT

North America’s year-to-date EBIT margin was 8.2%. More than half of the quarterly shortfall was linked to the 9% sales decline, while freight and distribution costs were 2% of the profit-and-loss statement higher year over year on a year-to-date basis.

North American Startups Still Need Adjustments

The Hammond and Paris, Texas, startups continued to require operational changes. Hammond is shifting toward simpler 12- and 18-count egg formats, while Paris is adjusting product specifications, formats, and operator processes for its new print line.

Foodservice Demand Remained Weak

Foodservice Packaging demand stayed well below last year’s level. Management said the segment must improve its top line, strengthen its growth pipeline, and become more successful at identifying new areas of expansion.

Contract Benefit Will Not Repeat

The quarter included EUR 23 million of revenue recognition from a commercial contract in smooth molded fiber. Management said the contract added EBIT and estimated its year-to-date 2026 impact at EUR 4 million-EUR 6 million, a benefit that will not recur.

Input Costs Continued to Rise

Huhtamaki described direct and indirect input-cost increases as significant and accelerating, with much of the pressure linked to the Middle East crisis. Higher fuel prices and limited truck-driver availability also increased freight and distribution costs in North America.

Sacramento Production Was Suspended

The company suspended production of smooth molded fiber at its Sacramento facility in the United States. The move forms part of broader operational and footprint actions across challenged areas of the portfolio.

Currency Remained a Major Headwind

Although currency translation turned positive during the quarter, foreign exchange reduced year-to-date net sales by EUR 67 million and EBIT by EUR 4.7 million. Negative translation differences also reduced equity by approximately EUR 186 million.

Year-to-Date Free Cash Flow Declined

Free cash flow was EUR 79 million year to date, below the prior-year level. Management attributed the comparison mainly to timing effects and other bridge items rather than a fundamental deterioration in the business.

Finance Costs and Working Capital Increased

Quarterly finance costs were approximately EUR 17 million and described as slightly elevated. Working capital was also higher, mainly because the company held more raw materials in response to conditions linked to the Middle East crisis.

Some Long-Term Metrics Remain Below Target

Adjusted return on investments and comparable growth remain below Huhtamaki’s long-term ambitions, even after recent improvement in comparable sales. Management emphasized that the latest growth trend was encouraging but not yet sufficient to close every gap.

Fiber Foodservice Market Was Weaker

Within Fiber Packaging, foodservice markets served with cup carriers were weaker during the quarter. Management noted that this is the smallest of the segment’s three main markets, limiting its overall effect on the division.

Footprint Review Includes Factory Closure

Huhtamaki is reviewing performance on a plant-by-plant basis and considering broader footprint actions in Foodservice and North America. The company also disclosed the closure of a Flexible Packaging factory in Baddi, India.

Guidance and Near-Term Outlook

Management made no changes to its outlook or short-term risk assessment and retained its long-term 10%-12% adjusted EBIT margin ambition. North America is expected to recover from its 8.2% year-to-date margin toward above 10%, while Hammond should improve further in the next quarter and through the first half of 2027; Foodservice demand is likely to remain weak as its pipeline takes time to develop.

Huhtamaki’s call showed a company making progress in margins, cash generation, leverage, and its strongest businesses, even as weak North American and Foodservice markets limit momentum. Investors will likely focus on whether operational improvements, seasonal demand, and disciplined capital allocation can convert that resilience into broader earnings growth.

data.title: IAG Earnings Call Highlights Strong Revenue and Cash Generation
data.description:
International Consolidated Airlines Group, S.A. ((ICAGY)) has held its Q3 earnings call. Read on for the main highlights of the call.

International Airlines Group delivered a predominantly positive earnings call, highlighting record revenue, strong yields, industry-leading margins, robust bookings, improving loyalty earnings and lower net debt. These gains outweighed lower year-on-year profit, higher fuel and disruption costs, foreign-exchange pressure, intense competition and delayed aircraft deliveries.

Record Revenue and Solid Profitability

IAG reported third-quarter revenue growth of 4.5% to a record level, with yields rising across all markets. Operating profit reached €1.726 billion, producing a 17.7% margin, while the first-nine-month operating margin was 13.5%.

Broad-Based Revenue Growth

Passenger revenue increased by €334 million, led by strong yields, particularly on long-haul routes. Cargo revenue rose €60 million as better pricing offset lower volumes, while other revenue grew €81 million through IAG Loyalty and higher Iberia Maintenance activity.

Passenger Unit Revenue Strength

Passenger unit revenue increased 4.1%, or 4.3% at constant currency, despite a 0.2% capacity decline. The North Atlantic was the standout region, with unit revenue up 11% on broadly unchanged capacity.

Regional Markets Remained Resilient

Latin America unit revenue rose 2.3%, or 3.4% at constant currency, as capacity expanded 5.4%. Africa, the Middle East and South Asia delivered a 13.2% unit-revenue increase with capacity down 19%, while Asia Pacific grew 3.8% on 9.3% higher capacity.

British Airways Led the Portfolio

British Airways generated £600 million of operating profit at a 14.4% margin, with unit revenue up 5.8%. Business revenue increased about 14% year over year in the quarter, supported by particularly strong North Atlantic performance.

All Airlines Posted Double-Digit Margins

Aer Lingus delivered €142 million of operating profit at a 17.4% margin, while Iberia produced €452 million at 19.6%. Vueling reported €257 million at a group-leading 23.8% margin, meaning every IAG airline achieved a double-digit quarterly margin.

IAG Loyalty Continued Its Expansion

IAG Loyalty operating profit increased 8% in the quarter, with underlying pre-HMRC profit rising £20 million to £171 million. The core loyalty business grew 20%, reinforcing its role as an increasingly important source of earnings diversification.

Cost Transformation Limited Inflation

Reported nonfuel unit costs rose 3.4%, but underlying nonfuel CASK increased only about 0.5% after adjusting for capacity, third-party maintenance, disruption and foreign exchange. Management pointed to tighter recruitment and stronger controls over suppliers, technology, artificial intelligence and discretionary spending.

Vueling Improved Costs and Customer Scores

Vueling’s transformation program, covering suppliers, specifications and technology, supported its cost performance. Its Net Promoter Score increased four points, while Spanish domestic capacity grew 7.3% and the airline retained a strong market position.

Debt Fell as Cash Generation Strengthened

Net debt declined to €4.2 billion from €4.7 billion at the half year and €5.9 billion at the end of the previous year. Net leverage fell 0.6 times, gross leverage stood at 1.9 times, and management expects 2026 free cash flow of about €3 billion.

Shareholder Returns Increased

IAG raised its interim dividend per share by 10% and continued its €1.5 billion share buyback program. Management also confirmed that the 2026 buyback program is being completed, underscoring confidence in the group’s balance sheet and cash generation.

Demand and Bookings Stayed Strong

The group was 85% booked for expected fourth-quarter demand, while bookings for the first quarter of 2027 were described as very strong. Passenger RASK was improving above third-quarter levels, with positive or resilient trends across the North Atlantic, Iberia, Latin America, Europe and domestic markets.

Corporate Travel Remained Robust

Corporate demand continued to perform well, led by technology and banking customers. British Airways reported strength among finance companies, technology firms and smaller businesses, along with healthy connecting traffic between the United States and India.

Fuel Recovery Made Progress

IAG expects to recover more than 80% of its full-year fuel costs, while British Airways is expected to recover over 100%. British Airways’ third-quarter fuel pass-through was about 75%, and management said pricing power remained strong in several markets.

Capacity and Fleet Plans Became More Disciplined

IAG reduced winter capacity in a measured effort to protect revenue and profitability. Full-year aircraft deliveries were cut to 12 from 16, while capital expenditure is now expected to be about €3.1 billion, below the previous €3.4 billion guidance.

Fleet and Product Investments Advanced

The group received its first Boeing 787-10 with GE engines in mid-October. British Airways’ new Club cabin retrofit was 82% complete at Heathrow, and the carrier aims to have Starlink installed on at least half of its long-haul fleet by year-end.

Investment Across the Airline Portfolio

IAG is continuing to invest in aircraft, customer initiatives and digital capabilities. Iberia plans cabin retrofits from 2027, Aer Lingus expects new business-class and premium-economy retrofits next year, and British Airways is planning a new First cabin on A380 and 777-9 aircraft from 2028.

Engine Business Set for Expansion

ITOCHU is investing in IAG Engine Tech after Iberia Maintenance won a LEAP engine license. The business plans to increase activity from about 200 engines annually to at least 350, backed by €400 million of investment and the recruitment of roughly 400 mechanics and engineers.

Aer Lingus Transformation Continued

Aer Lingus reported progress in head-office savings, digital revenue tools, supplier costs and the rollout of Starlink. One-third of senior managers had already left as part of the head-office cost-reduction program, reflecting the scale of the restructuring effort.

Funding and Hedging Remained Strong

IAG said it was not facing specific concerns in aircraft funding markets and was increasing the unencumbered share of its fleet. About 45% of 2027 fuel needs were hedged, with most protection linked to gas oil and jet fuel rather than Brent crude.

Operating Profit Declined Year Over Year

Third-quarter operating profit was €1.7 billion, down €327 million from the prior year’s record quarter. Operating profit before exceptional items for the first nine months fell 11% to €3.5 billion, showing that strong revenue did not fully offset higher costs.

Lower Profit and Adjusted Earnings

Profit after tax before exceptional items declined 12% to €2.4 billion in the first nine months. Adjusted earnings per share fell 9.2% to €0.154, with the lower profit only partly offset by the reduced share count created by the buyback program.

Fuel Costs Were a Major Headwind

Fuel costs increased €565 million in the third quarter as the Middle East conflict pushed jet fuel prices higher, although hedging provided some protection. Fuel unit costs jumped 30.7%, contributing to a 10.5% increase in total unit costs.

Nonfuel Expenses Also Increased

Nonfuel costs rose €163 million, with nonfuel unit costs up 3.4%. Employee unit costs increased 3%, supplier unit costs rose 2.9%, and ownership unit costs climbed 6.8%, adding pressure despite the group’s efficiency programs.

Operational Disruptions Raised Costs

Air traffic control outages, Heathrow baggage-system failures and unusually high Iberia engine costs added about 0.5 percentage points to nonfuel unit-cost growth. Lower-than-planned capacity contributed another 1.1 points, while greater third-party maintenance activity at Iberia added 1 point.

British Airways Faced Cost Pressure

British Airways’ nonfuel unit costs increased 5.1%, reflecting lower-than-planned capacity after repeated delays to the Middle East restart. Operational inefficiencies, NATS air traffic control outages and Heathrow baggage-system failures also weighed on the carrier’s performance.

Foreign Exchange Reduced Results

Foreign exchange was a €30 million net headwind in the third quarter because the weaker U.S. dollar reduced reported revenue. Management expects currency movements to remain a cost-side headwind in the fourth quarter, although they should provide support on the revenue side.

Middle East Disruption Limited Capacity

Third-quarter capacity was flat instead of the previously planned growth of about 1%, reflecting Middle East disruption, flight cancellations and U.K. air traffic control issues. IAG also expects some capacity to remain below original plans because aircraft redeployment from the region has been difficult.

Aircraft Deliveries Were Delayed

Expected 2026 deliveries were reduced to 12 from 16, with three Vueling Boeing 737s and one British Airways A321neo moving into 2027. The Boeing 777-9 is now expected in 2028, and management warned that further slippage could affect subsequent years.

Aer Lingus Faces Competitive Pressure

Aer Lingus expects a challenging competitive environment, with Ryanair announcing about 15% capacity growth for next summer. The North Atlantic market is also still absorbing a 50% capacity increase accumulated over recent years.

Vueling Saw Softer Leisure Demand

Leisure demand at Vueling was relatively soft through most of the summer, although trading improved from September. The airline nevertheless maintained its market position and continued to benefit from its transformation program.

European Competition Intensified

IAG described intra-European markets as highly competitive, with substantial capacity growth from rivals. The group reduced European capacity by 1.2% to protect profitability, prioritizing returns over volume in a crowded market.

Iberia Absorbed Engine Maintenance Costs

Iberia faced higher-than-expected engine maintenance challenges during the quarter. Airline-level nonfuel unit costs improved slightly by 0.3%, but unusually high engine-related expenses were identified as a one-off headwind.

Leverage Could Rise Seasonally

Management expects leverage to increase by year-end as seasonal booking patterns affect cash collection. The impact of seven aircraft deliveries expected in the following quarter will also increase capital expenditure and temporarily weigh on leverage.

2027 Capacity Growth Will Be Limited

IAG expects 2027 capacity growth to remain below mid-single digits, although the timing will depend partly on developments in the Middle East. The restrained plan reflects management’s focus on balancing demand, profitability and fleet availability.

Aer Lingus Margin Faced Seasonal Pressure

Aer Lingus produced a strong 17.4% margin in the seasonal quarter, but the result was lower than a year earlier. Management acknowledged the impact of increased competition while the airline continues to adapt its cost structure.

Forward-Looking Guidance

Management maintained its expectation for a full-year operating margin of at least 12%, significant free cash flow and about €3 billion of free cash flow in 2026, while ruling out a negative free-cash-flow scenario in 2026 or 2027. Fuel recovery is expected to exceed 80% groupwide and 100% at British Airways, with 2027 capacity growth below mid-single digits.

The group expects passenger RASK to remain above third-quarter levels, while lower disruption should support nonfuel CASK in the fourth quarter and foreign exchange should remain mixed. IAG now expects 12 aircraft deliveries and about €3.1 billion of capital expenditure for the year, with roughly 45% of next year’s fuel needs hedged.

Overall, IAG’s call showed a business with strong pricing power, resilient demand and improving financial flexibility, even as profits declined from an exceptional prior-year comparison. Investors will be watching fuel, disruption, competition and fleet delays, but continued cash generation, shareholder returns and disciplined capacity planning leave the group on a constructive footing.
